summary: The Monday sales meeting for the week, running about 59 minutes. Chris Klevan takes wins, then works through last week's numbers rep by rep — Andrew Musial, Richard Claessen, Michael Brideau and setter Kim Forbes-Sobers — reallocating missed revenue across future weeks on a shared projections board. He teaches the team the reporting format he wants going forward (slots booked, shows, closes, deposits, dominant objection) and diagnoses each rep's focus area. The last ten minutes cover marketing (retargeting-only ads, a VSL in production, an Instagram content ramp) and the $200/month Primal University price anchor appearing on calls. The meeting then closes out to a smaller group and becomes a call review of Andrew's Dan Keogh close, where Chris teaches the open-wallet doctrine, argues against volunteering payment plans, and coaches recommending a credit card as the funding route.
notable: DEPOSITS ARE COUNTED AS CLOSED UNITS IN THE REPORTED CLOSE RATE — Chris on Richard's week: 'so you had two deposits, one unit, so that's technically three people that committed. Are any of those deposits going to come Both.' then 'that's technically three units, right?' and 'So then you close three out of nine, so that's 33%, essentially.' Richard pushes back twice — 'No, they're not in yet' — and is overruled with 'No, but you said you're going to get them in, yeah?' The headline close rate for the week is therefore built on money that has not arrived, from deposits described elsewhere in the same meeting as unlikely to convert.

A DEPOSIT WAS TAKEN FROM A PROSPECT WITH A NEGATIVE BANK BALANCE — Richard, reporting his week: 'Dick had two deposits, even one from a guy that had minus 67 bucks in his account when I had to call with him. So I feel like I did okay with that lead.' It is offered as evidence of good work and passes without comment from the manager.

A DEPOSIT WAS TAKEN FROM A PROSPECT WHO WAS OVERHEARD SAYING HE HAD NO INTENTION OF BUYING — Andrew stayed connected on a phone line after closing Zoom and heard the prospect tell his wife 'oh yeah, I had to pay this guy, but I don't think he will [buy]. He just made me a courtesy.' Chris's response was 'Yeah, sometimes people will do that.' Andrew is separately still holding a $100 deposit from another prospect who got scared, and the reason given for returning it is exposure, not the customer: 'one, you're not getting any commission on it, two, if they get super scared and they don't want to get on the phone with you again, then they might just charge it back.'

THE SIX-MONTH INSTALMENT PLAN IS $1,200 A MONTH — $7,200 AGAINST A $6,000 HEADLINE — heard twice: Andrew describing the Dan Keogh close, 'he could do six times. 1,200', and in the played recording itself, 'we can do the six months, but it's going to be, like, 1,200 per month.' The prospect on that recording had just spent $300,000 cash on a house and said 'I don't have any cash'. No total was stated to him on the recording played.

REPS ARE TAUGHT TO DENY THAT SET PAYMENT PLANS EXIST — Chris, teaching the open-wallet play verbatim: 'So look, everything we do is custom. We don't have any sort of set payment plans at all. It just really depends on what we can make work with the person. So Trevor gives us a lot of flexibility because he really doesn't want to put people in a tough spot.' This is said in the same conversation in which a standard six-by-$1,200 structure is discussed as routine. It matches instruction recorded in Ben Byrne's 1-1 with the same manager a month earlier.

CONSUMER FINANCING IS ROUTINE, WITH RETRIES AFTER DECLINE — the team uses a lender referred to as PAVA plus PayPal and PayPal Credit. Chris's first response to a declined application is 'Did you try PayPal Credit too?' Andrew reports two declines in one weekend, one of them 'kind of a student, I think'; Richard reports a prospect with a $2,000 credit limit 'only got approved for 1,000, but of course not for six'. Chris: 'I don't know why they declined some people and some people they don't.' Andrew is sourcing an additional lender — 'I will send you today the name of, that I promised you, the, of the financing company' — and 'We have a couple of different financing partners, so we're looking at a split end.'

CREDIT CARD DEBT IS THE TAUGHT FUNDING ROUTE — Chris: 'when you find out they have the cash, you're like, okay, dude, like, can I tell you what I would do if I were you? Yeah, I would pay all front. I would do the whole thing. I'd put it on that credit card.' Andrew applied it: 'he told me his credit score was 700-something, and I was like, dude, put it on a credit card.' Richard states on the record that he is uncomfortable doing it: 'I understand the whole doing the open wallet, but then advising someone and putting it on a credit card... I've love. It's taught you need to be able to pay it off without a credit card, but that's something I need to work on myself, too.'

OPEN WALLET IS MANDATORY AND PREMISED ON THE PROSPECT HAVING THE MONEY — 'whenever it's finances, unless they straight up tell me, dude, I have the money to piff, I always open wallet. Always. No matter what.' The posture being praised is described by Chris as 'he's like, yeah, everybody says that, but I know you got the money. All right, dude, we just gotta find it.' The scripted transition harvests the full financial picture: cash, cards, available credit, credit score.

PROSPECTS ARE IDENTIFIED BY SEXUAL ORIENTATION AND NATIONALITY IN A RECORDED MANAGEMENT MEETING — Andrew refers to prospects as 'the gay guy', 'Tom, the gay one', 'the Dutch guy' and 'Eddie, the Asian guy'. Chris adopts the same terms rather than correcting them: 'Because you did have a hat trick, so did you pressure all three of the gay guys?'

AN AUTOMATED AGENT NAMED SOPHIA CONTACTS BOOKED LEADS AND MISFIRED — 'Sales kick was a bit wonky. Sophia was going rogue, doing some really weird stuff. It wouldn't be surprised if a lot of people were a little bit upset about that.' The remediation script is the only place its nature is disclosed to prospects: 'look, I know that the bot is kind of on the fritz a little bit and I'm really sorry about that... just ignore her and confirm with me.' Closers were told to confirm their own calls manually in the meantime.

THE $200/MONTH PRIMAL UNIVERSITY PRICE IS PUBLISHED AND IS ANCHORING CLOSER CALLS — Richard: '200 a month. I had someone today and he read that online, so that's exactly what he expected... He said like, yeah, I wouldn't have booked a meeting if it was six grand because I just can't do that right now.' Chris confirms the fix is known and deprioritised: 'I've talked to the team about it. It's a lower priority because all of our focus is on marketing right now... it's not as simple as just switching it. There's a lot of zaps.' The sanctioned response is to downsell: 'we can still sell them yeah just get them primarily get them in the primary just explain that to them'.

A PROSPECT ARRIVED ANCHORED AT $3,000 — Richard on a hedge fund prospect: 'he expected three grand, and he said, like, if it was three grand, I would have done it, but I'm not doing six grand like this.' Same prospect opened with 'people try to close me on one call, it's not going to happen'. Richard did not go for a deposit.

MICHAEL BRIDEAU WAS RELEARNING THE PROCESS WHILE TAKING LIVE CALLS THIS WEEK — 'I spent probably over the last two days, probably about 12 hours, just sales training and just going through some calls and role-playing objections because I'm just like, bro, I feel like I'm so off... I probably should have taken a bit more time before hopping on calls, to be honest.' He reports eight calls, one close, and names discovery as still 'a little bit all over the place'. Directly relevant to how his calls in this period should be read.

Marketing state as of this date: ads run to warm retargeting traffic only, no cold traffic; Instagram moving from one post a day to 30 pieces a week; a VSL scripted and about to be shot; messaging being repositioned toward coaching rather than kettlebell content generally.

Operational: Kim Forbes-Sobers is the setter behind the KFS suffix and reports her own sets, show rate and close rate. She notes most of her recent sets routed to Andrew. Daily sales meetings have started; Monday is the deep-dive on last week and the other days are pace checks plus training.

Rep language for a no-show/hang-up: Andrew initially read a dropped call as a hang-up, and it turned out to be a dead phone — 'he actually didn't hang up. He texted me that his phone was dead.' Chris had assumed the worse reading: 'this guy's either a really good actor or it's legit. And I kind of leaned on the side of like, he might just be a really good actor.'
